info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 6.3: AI-Assisted Normalization and the Risk of Over-Normalization.

questiontext.text: What is the central methodological question when evaluating generative AI for historical text normalization?

generalfeedback.text: The question is whether contextual capability is worth the fidelity and accountability it costs — not simply which method is more accurate.

answer.text: Whether the contextual disambiguation capability AI brings is worth the loss of transparency, reproducibility, and the risk of over-normalization.

feedback.text: Correct. The evaluation is not simply about raw accuracy, but balancing contextual power against editorial fidelity and inspectability.

answer.text: Whether language models can physically replace human eyes for reading damaged ink.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Today's task addresses linguistic normalization of transcribed text, not physical image transcription.

answer.text: Whether AI models can automatically rewrite historical texts in modern English.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Normalization regularizes historical orthography, not translating languages.

answer.text: Whether AI models can eliminate the need for version control in digital editions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Version control is essential for recording provenance and tracking changes across all methods.

name.text: 02 Question: Neural Normalization: The Sequence-to-Sequence Approach

questiontext.text: Why is training a character-level sequence-to-sequence model (such as a bi-LSTM) impractical for a single-folio term project?

generalfeedback.text: Neural normalization is framed as character-level translation and works well with data — which you do not have at the scale it needs.

answer.text: Neural sequence-to-sequence models require thousands of aligned training pairs to learn character transformations, which a single folio cannot provide.

feedback.text: Correct. Character-based translation models starve for data on small samples, requiring extensive historical corpora to achieve acceptable accuracy.

answer.text: Bidirectional LSTM networks are incapable of reading Greek characters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Bi-LSTMs handle arbitrary Unicode character vocabularies effectively when trained on sufficient data.

answer.text: Sequence-to-sequence models only run on supercomputers with quantum processors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Bi-LSTMs run on standard hardware; the constraint is training data volume.

answer.text: TEI guidelines strictly forbid the use of recurrent neural networks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI guidelines govern XML encoding standards, not machine learning architectures.

name.text: 03 Question: Data Sparsity and Multi-Task Learning

questiontext.text: What empirical finding characterizes multi-task learning in historical text normalization?

generalfeedback.text: Multi-task learning helps only around 5,000 tokens and degrades with abundant data — manuscript work is always the sparse regime.

answer.text: It provides significant error reduction when target data is exceptionally small (~5,000 tokens), but can degrade performance on abundant data due to domain mismatch.

feedback.text: Correct. Auxiliary tasks (like grapheme-to-phoneme mapping) help only in sparse-data regimes and harm performance when abundant target data is available.

answer.text: It guarantees 100% accuracy on every historical language without exception.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Multi-task learning reduces error rates under sparsity, but never guarantees perfect accuracy.

answer.text: It completely eliminates the need for human editors to review normalization outputs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Human review remains mandatory to verify philological validity.

answer.text: It only functions when the auxiliary task is written in modern English.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Auxiliary tasks typically involve related dialects, historical phonetics, or phonetic transcriptions.

questiontext.text: What capability do large language models bring to normalization that character-level rule scripts structurally lack?

generalfeedback.text: Models bring exactly the contextual capability your rules structurally lack — and lose exact character alignment and verifiability doing it.

answer.text: Paragraph-level attention that enables contextual and syntactic disambiguation of ambiguous historical forms.

feedback.text: Correct. Language models attend across surrounding sentences to determine grammatical roles that isolated token rules cannot discern.

answer.text: Guaranteed mathematical verifiability for every character transformation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Language models are probabilistic black boxes lacking the mathematical inspectability of rule transducers.

answer.text: Flawless character-level alignment between diplomatic and regularized forms in strict TEI.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Models frequently struggle with exact character-level alignment in structured markup.

answer.text: Total immunity from hallucinating non-existent words.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Generative models are prone to hallucination and lexical substitution without strict constraints.

questiontext.text: What is the specific danger of over-normalization when using generative models on historical manuscripts?

generalfeedback.text: Over-normalization produces better text than the manuscript contains — fluent, standard, and no longer a record of what was written.

answer.text: The model prioritizes modern fluency over diplomatic fidelity, silently altering dialectal syntax, replacing archaic lexemes, or erasing valid variants.

feedback.text: Correct. Over-normalization produces 'better', more standard text than the scribe wrote, destroying authentic linguistic and transmission evidence.

answer.text: The model crashes the local computer by generating infinite XML tags.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Over-normalization is a semantic and philological failure, not a computational crash.

answer.text: The model converts all Greek letters into Latin transliterations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The model generates Greek, but standardizes it excessively toward classical or modern norms.

answer.text: The model deletes all punctuation marks and line breaks from the TEI header.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Over-normalization affects textual words and grammar, not header metadata.

questiontext.text: Why must the entire diplomatic text—including standard forms—be supplied to the model during the normalization experiment?

generalfeedback.text: Supply the whole text, not just flagged tokens — a model that never sees a token cannot demonstrate over-application.

answer.text: Supplying only flagged non-standard tokens makes it impossible to measure over-application and false positives on standard words.

feedback.text: Correct. To evaluate whether a model inappropriately alters valid historical words, it must be given the opportunity to process the entire text.

answer.text: Language models refuse to process prompts that contain fewer than 500 words.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Models accept prompts of arbitrary length; full text is required for experimental validity.

answer.text: Standard Greek words are legally required to accompany historical variants.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The requirement is methodological and scientific, not legal.

answer.text: Supplying partial text causes Git to reject the subsequent commit.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git tracks whatever files are committed; experimental integrity requires the complete text.

questiontext.text: Why is the model explicitly prompted to classify the type of variation (e.g., orthographic, dialectal, name, slip)?

generalfeedback.text: Requiring the model to state the type of variation forces the editorial judgement into the open where it can be checked.

answer.text: It forces the model's underlying editorial classification into the open where it can be audited against the editor's policy.

feedback.text: Correct. Requiring a typed rationale allows the editor to check whether the model recognized an authentic dialectal form or mistook it for an error.

answer.text: The type attribute is required for Python to parse JSON strings.

feedback.text: Incorrect. JSON parsers handle arbitrary keys; the type field is an editorial audit mechanism.

answer.text: Classifying variation type automatically translates the text into modern English.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Classification identifies historical linguistic categories, not translations.

answer.text: The type field allows the model to bypass character token limits.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Token limits are architectural constraints unaffected by JSON keys.

questiontext.text: Why must raw model proposals be committed to Git before any editorial review or correction takes place?

generalfeedback.text: Commit the raw proposals before reviewing, and do not inject them into the TEI — the model proposes, you dispose.

answer.text: It preserves the unedited machine output as an auditable baseline, ensuring performance and error rates are measured accurately.

feedback.text: Correct. Reviewing before committing blends human corrections with machine proposals, destroying the empirical evaluation.

answer.text: Git automatically fixes any hallucinations in the JSON file during the commit process.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git records file states exactly as written without modifying content.

answer.text: Unreviewed commits are required to generate Moodle XML question banks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Question banks are generated from curated Python data modules.

answer.text: Committing raw output automatically publishes the text to academic journals.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Commits are private local repository milestones until pushed and published.

questiontext.text: Why are fidelity metrics (over-normalization rate, name violations, dialect collapse) essential alongside precision and recall?

generalfeedback.text: Compute over-normalization, name violation, and dialectal collapse rates — precision and recall alone cannot show a model is modernizing rather than regularizing.

answer.text: Precision and recall alone measure agreement with targets but fail to reveal whether the model is modernizing historical text and erasing linguistic data.

feedback.text: Correct. A model can achieve high precision while quietly erasing rare dialectal forms and modernizing archaic vocabulary.

answer.text: Fidelity metrics are the only numbers accepted by the TEI header parser.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI headers store descriptive prose and arbitrary metadata.

answer.text: Precision and recall cannot be calculated when comparing three methods.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Precision and recall are calculated pairwise across methods.

answer.text: Fidelity metrics measure the computational speed and GPU power used during inference.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Fidelity metrics evaluate philological integrity and text preservation.

name.text: 10 Question: Using the Baseline as a Detector

questiontext.text: How does the rule-based baseline detect generative over-normalization in language model proposals?

generalfeedback.text: Proposals unreachable by any character-level rule are where the model stopped regularizing orthography — that is the detector.

answer.text: Because rules only perform character-level substitutions, model proposals with large edit distances from rule reachability flag semantic or morphological alteration.

feedback.text: Correct. When a model proposal cannot be reached by character rewrite rules, it has almost certainly substituted a modern synonym or altered grammar.

answer.text: The rule baseline uses an online web crawler to check if the AI violated copyright law.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The detector uses string distance and rule reachability, not web crawlers.

answer.text: The rule baseline automatically deletes the AI model from the computer.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The baseline is a diagnostic filter that alerts the human editor to inspect suspicious proposals.

answer.text: The rule baseline converts all neural proposals into random Latin characters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The baseline performs mathematical distance analysis on Greek text.

questiontext.text: Why must an editor inspect high-deviation flagged cases individually rather than rejecting them automatically?

generalfeedback.text: Inspect flagged cases individually — some are gaps in your rules, and some are the model quietly removing evidence Week 7 needs.

answer.text: Some flagged cases may represent genuine orthographic variation that the rule set missed, while others represent destructive over-normalization.

feedback.text: Correct. Flagged proposals can reveal valid gaps in the editor's rules as well as harmful model hallucinations or lexical substitutions.

answer.text: Individual inspection is required by the computer operating system to release disk space.

feedback.text: Incorrect. File space is managed by the OS independently of editorial inspection.

answer.text: All flagged proposals are guaranteed to be 100% correct.

feedback.text: Incorrect. High-deviation proposals are precisely where models most frequently over-normalize or hallucinate.

answer.text: Automated rejection causes Git to corrupt the commit history DAG.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git history is unaffected by editorial acceptance or rejection.

questiontext.text: When evaluating how a language model resolves contextually ambiguous tokens, what must be assessed in addition to its final answer?

generalfeedback.text: Check whether correct resolutions come with genuine contextual reasons — a right answer without the reasoning has not demonstrated the capability.

answer.text: Whether the model provided a valid contextual and syntactic explanation rather than asserting a standard form based on frequency alone.

feedback.text: Correct. A correct answer with a generic explanation may be a lucky guess; genuine contextual disambiguation demonstrates syntactic reasoning.

answer.text: Whether the model generated the answer in less than one millisecond.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Inference speed does not validate linguistic reasoning.

answer.text: Whether the model used uppercase letters for all Greek words.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Greek casing conventions follow orthographic standards, not reasoning quality.

answer.text: Whether the model can translate the passage into five modern languages.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Multilingual translation is irrelevant to Greek contextual disambiguation.

questiontext.text: What is the 'downstream paradox' identified by Robertson and Goldwater regarding neural historical text normalization?

generalfeedback.text: Neural normalization generalizes well and may deliver no downstream benefit over memorization — which is why auditing against a rule baseline is the recommended practice.

answer.text: Neural models generalize well to unseen variants, but they do not consistently yield significant downstream NLP improvements over a naive memorization baseline.

feedback.text: Correct. Despite theoretical advantages, sophisticated neural normalizers often fail to improve downstream tagging more than simple lookup tables.

answer.text: Downstream parsers always crash when processing regularized Greek text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Parsers operate effectively on standard forms; the paradox concerns the relative gain over memorization.

answer.text: Normalizing text makes it completely impossible to perform lexical searches.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Normalization enables lexical search; the paradox concerns downstream POS tagging gains.

answer.text: Neural models refuse to process text that contains downstream XML milestones.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The paradox is an empirical NLP finding, not an XML formatting bug.

questiontext.text: How does lightweight retrieval-augmented grounding (RAG) reduce the risk of over-normalization in language models?

generalfeedback.text: Supplying candidates from your own lexicon constrains the model to attested forms — a lightweight grounding that removes much of the over-normalization risk.

answer.text: Supplying candidates from a project lexicon and policy constraints restricts the model to attested forms, preventing out-of-vocabulary hallucinations and modernizations.

feedback.text: Correct. Grounding anchors the model's generation in verified historical vocabulary and explicit editorial rules.

answer.text: RAG permanently disconnects the computer from the local area network.

feedback.text: Incorrect. RAG structures prompt context; it does not disable networking.

answer.text: RAG replaces the need for any human editorial review of the text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Grounded proposals still require human verification against the manuscript.

answer.text: RAG converts the entire TEI XML file into uncompressed audio files.

feedback.text: Incorrect. RAG operates entirely on text and structured data.

name.text: 15 Question: Direct TEI Generation and Its Failure

questiontext.text: What is the most dangerous failure mode when prompting a language model to generate TEI <choice> markup directly?

generalfeedback.text: A model-generated <orig> that has been partly normalized destroys the diplomatic layer silently — check it character by character.

answer.text: The model silently regularizes the <orig> element, permanently corrupting the diplomatic record without leaving visible traces.

feedback.text: Correct. If <orig> is altered, the diplomatic layer ceases to reflect the manuscript, silently destroying primary evidence.

answer.text: The model outputs well-formed XML that passes all schema validation checks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Well-formed valid XML is desirable; the danger is corrupted diplomatic text within valid tags.

answer.text: The model adds too many comments explaining historical Greek grammar.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Excessive commentary is a minor formatting issue, not a destruction of primary evidence.

answer.text: The model compiles the TEI file into a PDF document automatically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. PDF compilation is performed by external build tools, not model prompt outputs.

questiontext.text: What is the precise scholarly meaning of @resp="#llm" on an accepted <choice> regularization?

generalfeedback.text: @resp records what proposed a regularization, not what decided it — you decided all three classes, and nothing enters unreviewed.

answer.text: It indicates that the language model proposed the regularization, while the human editor reviewed and accepted responsibility for it.

feedback.text: Correct. @resp records proposal provenance; the editor remains accountable for every claim included in the edition.

answer.text: It declares that the model legally owns the copyright to that specific word.

feedback.text: Incorrect. @resp tracks scholarly provenance, not legal ownership.

answer.text: It informs downstream software that the word should be hidden from human readers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Regularized words are displayed in reading views regardless of proposal agent.

answer.text: It signals that the word was emended without consulting the manuscript facsimile.

feedback.text: Incorrect. All accepted proposals must be verified against the manuscript facsimile.

questiontext.text: In the comparative assessment of the three normalization methods, what unique guarantee does the rule script provide?

generalfeedback.text: The rule script *cannot* over-normalize, which is a guarantee rather than an observation — the model's equivalent cells must be measured.

answer.text: The rule script structurally cannot over-normalize or collapse dialectal forms, because it only performs character-level substitutions conditioned on lexicon presence.

feedback.text: Correct. The rule script's mathematical constraints guarantee that it cannot invent words or modernize syntax, whereas model outputs must always be tested.

answer.text: The rule script guarantees 100% recall across every folio of the manuscript.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Rule scripts often miss unseen variants, yielding moderate recall.

answer.text: The rule script eliminates the need to record provenance in the TEI header.

feedback.text: Incorrect. All methods require clear provenance declarations in the header.

answer.text: The rule script automatically resolves all contextually ambiguous Greek forms.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Rule scripts decline ambiguous tokens because they process tokens in isolation.

questiontext.text: What characterizes a rigorous, evidence-based conclusion in a normalization study?

generalfeedback.text: A hybrid conclusion derived from your own measurements is worth more than the same conclusion adopted from the literature.

answer.text: It provides specific quantitative metrics (precision, recall, over-normalization rate) and articulates a hybrid division of labor based on empirical findings.

feedback.text: Correct. A strong conclusion is quantified, acknowledges specific model failure modes, and recommends targeted hybrid workflows.

answer.text: It asserts that AI models have made human philologists completely obsolete.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Uncritical enthusiasm ignores documented failure modes and the necessity of human judgement.

answer.text: It claims that computers should never be used in digital humanities research.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Rejecting computational tools ignores the scalability and precision of hybrid pipelines.

answer.text: It copies verbatim paragraphs from commercial AI marketing brochures.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholarly conclusions must be grounded in primary empirical measurements.

questiontext.text: How does an editor practice methodological scepticism when integrating AI tools into a scholarly edition?

generalfeedback.text: Scepticism is a working practice — establish the standard, build a detector, constrain explicitly, measure fidelity, review everything, record provenance.

answer.text: By establishing ground truth first, building a baseline detector, constraining prompts, measuring fidelity, and reviewing all proposals before inclusion.

feedback.text: Correct. Scepticism is an active engineering and philological practice that guards the edition against unverified black-box claims.

answer.text: By refusing to turn on the computer or use digital text editors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digital methods are central to modern scholarship when properly disciplined.

answer.text: By accepting all model outputs without review to speed up publication.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Uncritical acceptance introduces silent errors and corrupts the diplomatic record.

answer.text: By deleting all documentation so readers cannot inspect how the text was made.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hiding methods creates a black box; scholarship requires full transparency.

questiontext.text: Why should the TEI header's <editorialDecl> describe the human review protocol and error-detection methodology?

generalfeedback.text: Record the review practice, not only the methods — a reader needs to know that nothing entered unreviewed and how review was targeted.

answer.text: It demonstrates to readers that machine proposals were systematically audited, establishing the evidentiary reliability of the entire regularized layer.

feedback.text: Correct. Documenting the review protocol proves that no unverified machine claims entered the edition, ensuring academic credibility.

answer.text: It is required by search engines to index polytonic Greek characters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Search indexing operates on text content, not TEI editorial declarations.

answer.text: It automatically generates PDF companion notes without running build scripts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. PDF compilation requires dedicated software pipelines.

answer.text: It transfers legal liability for errors to the software developer.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Editorial declarations establish scholarly transparency, not legal liability.

questiontext.text: Why is a character-by-character check of model-generated <orig> elements a mandatory verification step?

generalfeedback.text: Check model-generated <orig> character by character — a silently normalized diplomatic layer is the failure that cannot be recovered from.

answer.text: A model that silently normalizes the <orig> layer destroys the primary diplomatic evidence in a way that cannot be recovered from the XML.

feedback.text: Correct. If the diplomatic layer is compromised, the edition ceases to be an authentic record of the manuscript witness.

answer.text: Checking characters is required to convert the file into an image format.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Character verification ensures textual fidelity, not image conversion.

answer.text: The Python interpreter crashes if an <orig> tag contains Greek accents.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Python processes accented Unicode characters without error.

answer.text: Unchecked <orig> tags are automatically deleted by Git after pushing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git preserves all committed text exactly as authored.

questiontext.text: Why is an apparently perfect (0%) over-normalization rate misleading if reported in isolation?

generalfeedback.text: An excellent over-normalization rate on a model that proposed almost nothing is meaningless — read fidelity measures alongside recall.

answer.text: A model that was over-constrained and proposed almost no regularizations will have zero over-normalizations while achieving near-zero recall.

feedback.text: Correct. Fidelity metrics must always be evaluated alongside recall; doing nothing yields zero errors but zero utility.

answer.text: A 0% over-normalization rate causes a division-by-zero error in Python.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Zero percentages are valid numbers; the issue is methodological interpretation.

answer.text: A 0% over-normalization rate proves that the model achieved super-human intelligence.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Zero over-normalization coupled with low recall simply reflects an inactive model.

answer.text: TEI guidelines require every edition to contain at least 10% erroneous regularizations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Editions strive for zero errors through rigorous human review.

name.text: 23 Question: What Good Work Looks Like Here

questiontext.text: What is the methodological difference between using the rule baseline as a competitor versus using it as a detector?

generalfeedback.text: Using the rule baseline as a detector — rather than merely as a competitor — is what makes today an audit rather than a comparison.

answer.text: A competitor merely compares aggregate accuracy scores, whereas a detector uses character reachability to actively audit and flag suspicious neural outputs.

feedback.text: Correct. Using the baseline as a detector turns the deterministic script into an active quality assurance instrument for evaluating AI.

answer.text: A competitor runs on a different computer, whereas a detector runs in the cloud.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both techniques run locally within the project evaluation pipeline.

answer.text: A detector automatically deletes any files created by the competitor.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The detector inspects and flags text tokens for human review.

answer.text: A competitor evaluates Latin text, while a detector evaluates Greek text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both apply across historical languages.

name.text: 24 Question: Connecting to the Weeks Ahead

questiontext.text: Why is the regularized layer created this week indispensable for Week 9's automated lemmatization and parsing?

generalfeedback.text: Week 7 must choose a layer to collate on — <reg> for substantive variants, <orig> for evidence of shared descent.

answer.text: Automated morphological parsers and digital lexicons fail on unnormalized historical phonetic spellings, requiring standard forms in <reg>.

feedback.text: Correct. Lexicons and parsers expect standard classical headwords; iotacistic spellings in raw text break morphological lookup.

answer.text: Morphological parsers only execute on files that have been published in print.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Parsers run on digital text files.

answer.text: Week 9 requires all Greek words to be converted into English translations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Lemmatization identifies Greek dictionary lemmas, not English translations.

answer.text: The regularized layer is used to calculate physical parchment thickness in Week 9.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Regularization addresses linguistic spelling, not codicological measurements.

name.text: 25 Question: The Week's Three Methods, Reviewed

questiontext.text: How do the three steps of Topic 6 relate to one another in the overall project architecture?

generalfeedback.text: Each method's limits define the next one's job — which is why none of the three steps is redundant.

answer.text: Each method's structural limitations define the next method's role: manual sets policy, rules provide verifiable baselines, and AI assists with context.

feedback.text: Correct. The cycle is non-redundant and hierarchical: each method addresses the specific blind spots of the preceding tool.

answer.text: The three steps are identical duplicates created to increase student homework volume.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Each step explores a distinct computational and philological paradigm.

answer.text: Only the AI step is kept in the final edition; the manual and rule steps are discarded.

feedback.text: Incorrect. All three steps contribute to the multi-layered edition and its documented provenance.

answer.text: The three methods are competing commercial software products licensed by the university.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They represent core methodologies in digital scholarly editing.

name.text: 26 Question: A Note on What Was Preserved

questiontext.text: What is the ultimate scholarly achievement of encoding regularizations in parallel TEI XML?

generalfeedback.text: Not one original form was overwritten — that is the week's actual achievement, and it came from ordinary decisions made deliberately.

answer.text: Not a single historical scribal spelling was overwritten, allowing diplomatic fidelity and modern computational searchability to coexist perfectly.

feedback.text: Correct. By refusing the false choice between diplomatic and critical texts, TEI preserves primary evidence while enabling modern research tools.

answer.text: The digital edition was compressed into a proprietary encrypted format.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI XML is an open, non-proprietary international standard.

answer.text: All manuscript spelling variations were eliminated from historical memory.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Variations are preserved permanently in <orig>.

answer.text: The need for human scholars to read manuscripts was permanently removed.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digital editions enhance and empower human philological research.

questiontext.text: What critical preparation must be completed during the Fall Study Break before Week 7's collation sessions?

generalfeedback.text: Use the study break to transcribe your second witness — Week 7's collation needs two witnesses and cannot proceed with one.

answer.text: Transcribing the corresponding lines of a second manuscript witness, since automated collation requires at least two witnesses to compare.

feedback.text: Correct. Collation aligns and compares multiple texts; without a second transcribed witness, collation cannot take place.

answer.text: Purchasing a commercial license for proprietary collation software.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The course uses open-source tools like CollateX.

answer.text: Memorizing the entire Greek New Testament in modern monotonic spelling.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholarship relies on critical editions and tools, not rote memorization.

answer.text: Deleting the Git repository to start Week 7 with a clean slate.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The repository must be preserved and expanded across the term.

name.text: 28 Question: What the Assignment Will Require

questiontext.text: Why is it strongly recommended to draft the over-normalization analysis immediately rather than waiting until the assignment due date?

generalfeedback.text: Write the over-normalization analysis today — the study break intervenes and reconstructing today's reasoning later is much harder.

answer.text: The Fall Study Break intervenes, and reconstructing today's empirical measurements and reasoning weeks later is substantially harder.

feedback.text: Correct. Documenting experimental findings while the comparison data and decision rationale are fresh ensures accurate reporting.

answer.text: Assignment reports submitted after today are subject to automatic deletion by Git.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git never deletes files automatically; immediate drafting preserves fresh analytical insights.

answer.text: The Python scripts will self-destruct once the study break begins.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Local scripts and repositories persist indefinitely.

answer.text: University servers block all assignment submissions during study breaks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Submissions and repositories remain fully accessible.

questiontext.text: Why is an explicit, documented normalization policy more valuable to future scholarship than an unstated traditional editorial standard?

generalfeedback.text: Stating the policy does not make it right; it makes it arguable, which is the condition under which it can be improved.

answer.text: An explicit policy makes editorial decisions arguable, testable, and improvable, whereas unstated practices conceal assumptions from scrutiny.

feedback.text: Correct. Transparency allows future scholars to understand, evaluate, and re-analyze editorial choices under different assumptions.

answer.text: An explicit policy guarantees that no future scholar will ever disagree with the text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholarship thrives on debate; explicit documentation provides the evidence needed for informed disagreement.

answer.text: Documented policies allow web browsers to display 3D animations of the manuscript.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Editorial documentation serves philological rigor, not 3D web animations.

answer.text: Unstated practices are strictly illegal under digital repository regulations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Documenting policy is a standard of scholarly excellence, not administrative regulation.

name.text: 30 Question: Synthesis: Fluency Against Fidelity, Again

questiontext.text: What is the ultimate lesson regarding generative AI models in textual scholarship?

generalfeedback.text: The model's failure mode is improvement rather than error, and improvement has no image to check against — which is why the verifiable baseline is the detector.

answer.text: Generative models fail through fluent 'improvement' rather than obvious errors, making verifiable deterministic baselines essential for detecting subtle alterations.

feedback.text: Correct. Because over-normalized text looks polished and standard, an inspectable rule baseline is required to catch where authentic historical evidence was erased.

answer.text: Generative models should be used without restriction for all scholarly editing tasks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Unrestricted models silently erase authentic linguistic and textual variation.

answer.text: Generative models are incapable of generating valid Greek words.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Models generate highly fluent Greek; the danger is that it is too fluent and unfaithful to the manuscript.

answer.text: Deterministic rule baselines are obsolete and should be replaced entirely by generative AI.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Verifiable rule baselines are the vital detector and check on opaque AI models.
